catalog_locator: Fraser 1891 p.74, phonology preamble, paragraph beginning 'The accent is generally on the penultimate vowel' (page image);…
catalog_quote: The accent is generally on the penultimate vowel, and runs on into the following consonant. The final vowel, in most cases, is very lightly touched. An exception to the general accent is when a word ends in a diphthong. In such cases the diphthongs are usually accented. When a word ends in io or iu the accent is generally on the vowel before them (i.e., these endings are only reckoned as single vowels.) The accented vowels have a long and a short (or a heavy and a light) sound. They are long before final i or u, and short before final a, e, or o ...

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on the held page image of Fraser 1891 p.74, and the m-prefix subrule is verbatim on p.85 and in Ray 1926 (held scanned). Deciding source: an 1891 25-page missionary grammar sketch, hedged ('generally', 'usually'), which is why the record is weight-hedged/QS-HEDGED with final diphthong (CVV) attracting accent, else penult. Best available: Glottolog lists only Fraser 1891 and Ray 1926 as descriptive works (both held); Lynch & Crowley 2001 (fetched sources now, pp.103-104) confirm these plus Ray 1888-89 are the only sketches and that Baki has no grammar or dictionary; no phonology/prosody study was found. So the record rests on the best existing description, held and quoted from a page image; it is 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced' only because the source itself is a brief 19th-century impressionistic statement, not because a better source is being ig
